1) Q: Is the material in the two bottles the same (same enrichment, same composition)? Use the Graded Decision Framework (GDF) to compare and assign a confidence level.

A1.2: Based on the U isotopic compositions and trace element concentrations - additional information provided in Inject 1b - we assess that the two samples are inconsistent with high confidence. Our assessment factored in the results of the graded decision framework (GDF) as well as expert knowledge of these kind of measurements.

U isotopic compositions are inconsistent, based on a p‐value determination for the provide U isotopic compositions. Univariate comparison between the two samples yielded p‐values for the 234‐U/238‐U, 235‐U/238‐U and 236‐U/238‐U of 9.41E‐08, 0, and 2.15E‐04, respectively. The p‐ value for the U assay comparison was 5.33E‐11. These p‐values, which are far less than the 0.05 decision threshold for consistency, indicate that the two samples are inconsistent with high confidence. This assessment is counter to the preliminary assessment based on the gamma spectroscopy data alone. The addition of higher precision mass spectrometry data - along with SME interpretation to fill information gaps - provides a more well‐informed assessment. We would like to note that the omission of standards data precludes us from drawing any conclusion about the accuracy of the data. Therefore, we assume that the higher precision mass spectrometry data should supersede the gamma spectrometry data in both accuracy and precision.

A point‐to‐point multivariate analysis as directed by the GDF of the trace element data yielded the following assessments. Based on GDF multivariate comparison, trace element data for both unknown samples provide us with the following information: 1) The majority of the elements (ranked 1‐40) are deemed inconsistent with high confidence, 2) Cd and Hf concentrations are deemed inconsistent with medium confidence, 3) Er, Sb, Cs, Tl, Be, K, Tb, Gd, Ca, Rb, B are deemed consistent. Li was not detected or analyzed in one of the samples, so we had no value to use for the calculation. Many of the trace element values for Sample 2 have zero reported for measurement uncertainty. Expert interpretation indicates these uncertainties are in fact either not reported or rounded to zero. The GDF requires measurement uncertainties, so these measurements cannot be evaluated with the GDF.

2) Q: Are the materials consistent with materials in your library, and what confidence do you have?

We assess with high confidence that the questioned materials are not consistent with any material in our library. Based on gamma and mass spectrometry results, the questioned materials are DU; there is no DU in our library. This evaluation assumes the comparator data in the database has less than ~50% uncertainty on the U‐235 wt% - no uncertainties were included - and that the UOC portion of the library only includes concentrated U ores of a natural origin.

Based on the U isotopes, the questioned materials (DU) are inconsistent with the UOC portion of the library. The UOC portion of the library does not provide isotopic information. Lacking this


<!-- Page 4 -->


information, we assume for this exercise that only material with natural U‐235 concentration is included in the UOC library.

Based on the U isotopes, as well as physical form - the unknowns are not pellets - the questioned materials are inconsistent with the Pellet Exemplars portion of the library. The pellet exemplars portion of the library includes U isotopics, but the lowest U‐235 concentration is natural uranium (NU).

The questioned materials are not consistent with the Radioactive Sources portion of the library because the only reported radionuclides in these unknowns are U isotopes, and this is inconsistent with radionuclides used in radioactive sources. We assume if fission or activation products above background levels had been detected during the initial RIID or gamma spectrometry analyses, they would have been reported.

The questioned materials are not consistent with any material in the Interdicted Materials portion of the library. There is no DU in this portion of the library.

Since a relatively pure DU blended with even a small amount of UOC would perturb the isotopics while retaining the trace element signature, we also considered a potential mixing scenario with material represented by the UOC in our library. Fuel pellets are typically much higher purity than UOC, but for completeness, we also considered the Fuel Pellets portion of the library. We used two different multivariate data visualization tools to compare trace element signatures in the unknowns to UOC and Fuel Pellet populations represented in our library.

First, we produced spider plots using averages for the uranium ore concentrates (UOCs) by deposit type as well as the pellets largely by reactor type. We found that plotting each sample individually lead to unnecessary complexity in the visualization of the spider plots. Typically, spider plots or (spidergrams) are used in geochemistry to plot element concentrations. Although these types of plots are often normalized to a known whole‐rock composition, we used our un‐ normalized results for comparison with the library purposes only.
